short_explanation: If N is on Alpha 1 (as the key assumes), the person immediately above N is O on Alpha 2, whom the key describes as the one west of Y; but the premises allow N to be on Alpha 5 as well, and they never say which flat lies west.
explanation_text: Every premise is satisfied by four arrangements: Z3, X4 in Flat Alpha and M5, S4, Y2, R1 in Flat Beta are fixed, but N and Q can occupy Alpha 1 and Alpha 5 either way round (both give N + Q = 6), and O and P can occupy Alpha 2 and Beta 3 either way round (both adjacent, both below S). The official key works from the arrangement with N on Alpha 1, Q on Alpha 5, P on Beta 3 and O on Alpha 2.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The one immediately below X is Z on Alpha 3, two floors above N (when N is on floor 1), not immediately above.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: S is on Beta 4, not immediately above N in any arrangement.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: R is on Beta 1, the same floor as N (or four floors below it), never above N.

solution_steps: Z is in Flat Alpha on an odd floor and two floors above R, who is in Flat Beta: Z3/R1 or Z5/R3.
M is in Flat Beta on floor 5; Y is also in Flat Beta with two floors between them, so Y is on Beta floor 2.
S is not in Z's flat, so S is in Flat Beta and X is in Flat Alpha on the same floor; S is not below Y, so S is on Beta 3 or Beta 4.
Floors above N = floors below Q means (5 - N) = (Q - 1), i.e. N + Q = 6.
Case Z5/R3: S must be Beta 4, X Alpha 4; the free slots are Beta 1, Alpha 3, 2, 1, and no two of them add to 6 for N and Q. Case rejected.

Case Z3/R1: Alpha 3 is Z, so S is Beta 4 and X is Alpha 4. Free slots: Alpha 5, Alpha 2, Alpha 1, Beta 3. N + Q = 6 forces N and Q into Alpha 1 and Alpha 5; O and P take Alpha 2 and Beta 3 (adjacent floors, both below S).

Result: Beta - M5, S4, (P or O)3, Y2, R1; Alpha - (Q or N)5, X4, Z3, (O or P)2, (N or Q)1. The premises do not fix which of N/Q is on floor 1 or which of O/P is in Beta 3; the answer key assumes N on Alpha 1, Q on Alpha 5, P on Beta 3, O on Alpha 2.
common_traps: Assuming Flat Alpha is west of Flat Beta: the stimulus never gives the flats' directions.
key_note: The stimulus leaves N/Q (Alpha 1 vs Alpha 5) and O/P (Alpha 2 vs Beta 3) interchangeable; all four arrangements satisfy every premise. With N on Alpha 1 the answer is the Alpha 2 occupant, which is option d only if Alpha is taken to be west of Beta (never stated); with N on Alpha 5 nobody is above N and option e holds. Competing options: d and e.

solution_steps: At break-even point, contribution = fixed cost = ₹60,000.
P/V ratio = contribution / sales = 60,000 / 1,50,000 = 0.40.

formula_used: P/V ratio = Fixed cost / Break-even sales × 100
common_traps: Trying to use the ₹12 variable cost per unit: without a selling price per unit it cannot be used.

topic_name: Linear row — single row, one direction
short_explanation: In the arrangement the key uses, E K M V R G A H, G sits immediately right of R.
explanation_text: Working from V gives two seatings that meet every clue: E K M V R G A H and K E V M G R H A. The second gives H as R's right neighbour, which is not among the options, so G is the only listed answer.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: A sits at seat 7, two to the right of R.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: V sits immediately left of R.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: M sits two to the left of R.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: K sits three to the left of R.

solution_steps: Number seats 1 to 8 from the left (west) end, since all face north.
G = V + 2, H = G + 2 = V + 4, and K is two seats from V on the side away from G, so K = V - 2. Hence V is 3 or 4.
V = 4: K2, G6, H8; A = 9 - K = 7; M beside V with E two to its left gives M3/E1 (R then takes seat 5) or M5/E3 (R would be left at seat 1, an end, so rejected). Arrangement: E K M V R G A H.
V = 3: K1, G5, H7; M must be 4 (M2 would put E off the row), E2; A = 9 - 1 = 8; R takes seat 6. Arrangement: K E V M G R H A, which also satisfies every clue (0 persons left of K, 0 right of A).
The answer key uses E K M V R G A H.
common_traps: Treating left and right as seen by the reader, not the persons facing north.
key_note: The premises allow two arrangements, E K M V R G A H (used by the key) and K E V M G R H A (zero persons left of K and right of A). Here the alternative gives H, which is not an option, so G stands.

solution_steps: Number seats 1 to 8 from the left (west) end, since all face north.
G = V + 2, H = G + 2 = V + 4, and K is two seats from V on the side away from G, so K = V - 2. Hence V is 3 or 4.
V = 4: K2, G6, H8; A = 9 - K = 7; M beside V with E two to its left gives M3/E1 (R then takes seat 5) or M5/E3 (R would be left at seat 1, an end, so rejected). Arrangement: E K M V R G A H.
V = 3: K1, G5, H7; M must be 4 (M2 would put E off the row), E2; A = 9 - 1 = 8; R takes seat 6. Arrangement: K E V M G R H A, which also satisfies every clue (0 persons left of K, 0 right of A).
The answer key uses E K M V R G A H.
key_note: The premises allow two arrangements, E K M V R G A H (used by the key) and K E V M G R H A (zero persons left of K and right of A). E K M V R G A H gives E, H (d); K E V M G R H A gives K, A, which only 'None of these' (e) covers. Competing options: d and e.

short_explanation: Settlement risk in foreign exchange is called Herstatt risk, after Bankhaus Herstatt, which failed in 1974 after receiving Deutsche Mark payments but before paying out the dollars it owed. One leg of a trade settles and the other does not.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Liquidity risk is being unable to fund or trade without loss, a separate concept.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Operational risk comes from failed processes, systems or people; it is not the name for forex settlement risk.

common_traps: Candidates choose credit risk because settlement risk is a kind of counterparty exposure, but the question asks for its specific name.

short_explanation: K <= G = C <= E = A gives K <= A, so I follows. III needs strict E > K but the chain only gives E >= K, and Z and S are linked through opposite signs, so II fails.

solution_steps: I: K <= G = C <= E = A => K <= A. True.
II: Z > C <= E >= S: signs oppose, no relation. False.
III: K <= G = C <= E => E >= K only, not E > K. False.
common_traps: Reading E >= K as E > K and choosing 'I and III'.

short_explanation: E = Y >= W >= C >= A gives E >= A, and B > W >= C >= A = U gives B > U. Y and S meet only through W = I < S with opposing signs, so III fails.

short_explanation: In property insurance, indemnity-based settlement values the loss at market value, i.e. replacement cost less depreciation. When the sum insured is below this actual (market) value, the claim is settled on market value and scaled down proportionately under the average clause.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Agreed value applies where insurer and insured fix the item's value in advance (e.g. art, vintage cars), so no under-valuation question arises.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Replacement or reinstatement value pays the cost of a new item without deducting depreciation; it is an alternative basis, not the one tied to actual value.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Depreciation is one element used in arriving at market value, not the basis of settlement itself.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Salvage value is what the damaged item realises, which is deducted from the claim; it is not a basis of settlement.

common_traps: The situation described is under-insurance, which triggers the average clause; candidates may look for 'average' and be thrown by its absence.
key_note: The stem describes under-insurance, whose settlement consequence is the average (pro-rata) condition, which is not offered. Market value is accepted as the indemnity valuation basis against which under-insurance is measured, but the wording is loose.

solution_steps: Mayank: non-technical 60, technical 60 + 30 = 90, total 200, so GK = 50.

Mayank's 200 is 5/6 of Isha's total ⇒ Isha total = 240.
Isha non-technical = 50 + 40 = 90; Isha technical = 1.2 × 70 = 84; Isha GK = 240 − 90 − 84 = 66.
Isha GK : Lalit GK = 3 : 2 ⇒ Lalit GK = 44.

solution_steps: Work backwards from the known terms: 45/18 = 2.5, 157.5/45 = 3.5, 708.75/157.5 = 4.5.

short_explanation: Both forwards and futures create a binding obligation to buy or sell gold at a set price on a future date. The key takes futures, which are standardised and traded on exchanges such as MCX, but the stem's phrase 'between two counterparties' describes a bilateral forward just as well.
explanation_text: Options give the holder a right, not an obligation, so they are out. Swaps exchange cash-flow streams and bonds are debt instruments, so neither fits. That leaves forwards and futures. A forward is a private OTC contract between two counterparties with terms tailored to them. A future is a standardised exchange-traded contract in which the clearing corporation stands between buyer and seller. Only the words 'on an exchange' or 'standardised' in the stem would make futures the clear answer.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Options give the buyer a right, not an obligation, to buy or sell.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Swaps exchange streams of cash flows; they are not the standard contract for buying gold at a fixed future price.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Bonds are debt instruments, not contracts to trade gold on a future date.

common_traps: Candidates overlook the word 'obligation', which rules out options, and then cannot choose between forwards and futures because the stem does not say whether the contract is exchange-traded.
key_note: Forwards (b) and futures (d) both fit. Each creates an obligation to trade gold at a fixed price on a future date, and 'between two counterparties' describes the bilateral OTC forward at least as well as an exchange-traded future. The stem does not mention standardisation or exchange trading, which would single out futures.

formula_used: ROE = Profit after tax (less preference dividend) / Equity shareholders' funds × 100
common_traps: ROCE also measures return on capital, but its base includes long-term debt.

topic_name: NPCI systems — UPI, IMPS, NEFT, RTGS
short_explanation: IMPS, the round-the-clock instant interbank fund transfer service launched in 2010, is owned and operated by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), the umbrella retail-payments body promoted by RBI and the Indian Banks' Association.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: RBI regulates and supervises payment systems under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, and itself operates RTGS and NEFT, but it does not operate IMPS.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: SEBI regulates the securities market and has no role in retail payment systems.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: IDRBT is RBI's banking-technology research and training institute; it earlier ran the INFINET network but does not operate IMPS.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: IBA is an association of banks and one of NPCI's promoters, not the operator of IMPS.

common_traps: Confusing the regulator with the operator: RBI authorises and oversees IMPS, but NPCI runs it; RBI directly operates only RTGS and NEFT.

topic_name: Commercial paper — eligibility and net worth
short_explanation: Commercial paper is an unsecured money-market promissory note issued by highly rated corporates (and eligible NBFCs and financial institutions) for maturities of 7 days up to one year.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Treasury bills are issued by the Government of India (in 91, 182 and 364-day tenors), not by companies.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Certificates of deposit are issued by banks and select financial institutions against deposits, not by companies in general.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Call money is overnight interbank borrowing and lending, not an instrument issued by companies.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Notice money is interbank borrowing for 2 to 14 days, not a company-issued instrument.

common_traps: Certificate of deposit has the same 7-day to one-year tenor for banks; the deciding word is the issuer, companies versus banks.

topic_name: Broad trends in the Union Budget
short_explanation: FDI in Indian insurance was raised from 26% to 49% in 2015 and to 74% in 2021. The Union Budget 2025-26 proposed raising it to 100% for insurers that invest the entire premium in India, with conditions to be prescribed.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 49% was the limit before 2021, not the Budget 2025-26 figure.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: 74% was the limit set in 2021, which the Budget 2025-26 raised further.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: The announcement attached conditions such as investing the entire premium in India, not mandatory Indian management control.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: 51% under composite foreign investment was never the insurance cap announced in the Budget.

common_traps: Choosing 74%, the limit in force before the 2025-26 Budget raised it to 100%.

topic_name: Percentage comparison — what percent of / more than
short_explanation: Take the Pencil as 100: the Pen is 80 and the Eraser is 80/1.2 = 66.67. The new Pencil cost is 110, and 110 / (80 + 66.67) = 110 / 146.67 = 75%.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 50% is how far the original Pencil (100) exceeds the Eraser (66.67), which compares the Pencil with the Eraser alone and skips both the 10% increase and the Pen.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: 80% is the Pen-to-Pencil figure given in the question, not the ratio asked for.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 90%; the working gives 75% (110/146.67).

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 105%; the working gives 75% (110/146.67).

solution_steps: Let the cost of the Pencil = 100, so Pen = 80% of 100 = 80.
Pen is 20% more than Eraser, so Eraser = 80/1.2 = 200/3 ≈ 66.67.
New Pencil cost = 100 × 1.1 = 110.
common_traps: Taking Eraser as 80% of the Pen (64) instead of dividing by 1.2; that gives about 76.4%.
Forgetting the 10% increase, which gives about 68.2%.

topic_name: Poverty alleviation and employment generation in India
short_explanation: The e-Shram portal, launched in 2021 by the Ministry of Labour and Employment, builds a national database of unorganised workers seeded with Aadhaar. That database is meant to deliver social security benefits transparently and to target welfare schemes on verified data, so all three statements are correct.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits Statements 2 and 3, which are also stated objectives of the portal.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits Statement 3; targeted welfare interventions based on verified data are also an objective.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits Statement 1; building the national database is the portal's founding objective.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Omits Statements 1 and 2, which are also objectives of the portal.

topic_name: Six Sigma — DMAIC, belts, defect level
short_explanation: DMAIC, the Six Sigma improvement cycle, is Define, Measure, Analyse, Improve, Control; D is Define.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 'Design' belongs to DMADV (Define, Measure, Analyse, Design, Verify), used for new processes.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: 'Direct' is not a Six Sigma phase.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 'Develop' is not a DMAIC phase.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: 'Determine' is not a DMAIC phase.

common_traps: DMADV also starts with Define; its D-words are Define and Design.

short_explanation: PFRDA was first set up in 2003 by a government resolution and got statutory status only when the PFRDA Act, 2013 was passed (notified in 2014).

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: PFRDA was set up in 2003 by an executive resolution, and the 2004 ordinance lapsed; neither gave it lasting statutory status.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: The PFRDA Bill was introduced in 2005 but lapsed and was never passed.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: There is no PFRDA Act of 2016.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Regulations are subordinate legislation made under the Act; they did not create the authority.

common_traps: Confusing the 2003 interim set-up or the 2005 Bill with the 2013 Act that gave PFRDA statutory status.

short_explanation: BRICS summits are hosted by the rotating chair, and Brazil chaired BRICS in 2025. The 17th BRICS Summit and the associated BRICS Business Forum were held in Rio de Janeiro in July 2025.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: China did not host the 2025 summit.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: South Africa hosted the 15th summit in 2023 (Johannesburg), not the 17th.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: India did not host the 2025 summit, and the option itself is an invalid city pairing.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Kazan hosted the 16th summit in 2024, not the 17th.

common_traps: Kazan, Russia hosted the previous (16th) summit in 2024; candidates recalling the most recent summit they read about may pick it.

short_explanation: When the futures price trades below the spot price, the market is in backwardation; the opposite, futures above spot, is contango.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Contango is the normal situation where the futures price is above the spot price, reflecting cost of carry.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Hedging is a strategy of offsetting risk, not a description of the futures-spot price relationship.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrage is exploiting a price discrepancy between markets, not the name of the price relationship itself.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Basis trading is a strategy built on the futures-spot gap, not the name of the condition where futures are below spot.

common_traps: Swapping contango and backwardation: remember contango is the usual cost-of-carry state (futures above spot), and backwardation is its reverse.

short_explanation: Since 2020, IFSCA is the single, unified regulator for all financial products, services and institutions in an IFSC, covering banking, capital markets, insurance, pensions and related services.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: RBI's IFSC powers were transferred to IFSCA; it no longer regulates services in the IFSC.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: The separate-regulator model was replaced precisely by the unified IFSCA.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Exchanges in the IFSC are regulated by IFSCA; they do not self-regulate alone.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: The World Bank is not a regulator of any jurisdiction.

short_explanation: W's rate is 1/28, so U and V together do 1/8 - 1/28 = 5/56 per hour. With U's time t and V's time 4t, 1/t + 1/(4t) = 5/(4t) = 5/56, so t = 14 hours.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 7 hrs is half of U's time; it does not satisfy 1/7 + 1/28 + 1/28 = 1/8.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 21 hrs; the working gives 14 hrs (5/(4t) = 5/56).

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 56 hrs is V's time (4 × 14), or U's time if the 1 : 4 ratio is reversed.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 35 hrs; the working gives 14 hrs (5/(4t) = 5/56).

solution_steps: Combined rate of U, V, W = 1/8 per hour; W's rate = 1/28.
Let U take t hours, so V takes 4t: 1/t + 1/(4t) = 5/(4t).
common_traps: Reading the 1 : 4 ratio as rates rather than times, which reverses who is faster and gives U = 56 hours.

topic_name: Process innovation and Business Process Re-engineering
short_explanation: The key contrasts BPR, which amends or reworks existing processes, with Process Innovation, described in the stem as renovating them. 'Amend' is the only option that does not simply repeat PI's word or name something other than changing a process.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 'Renovation' is the word the stem gives to Process Innovation, so it cannot also be BPR's focus.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: 'Reduce' describes cost cutting, not what BPR does to processes.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 'Remove' suggests eliminating processes outright; BPR redesigns them.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: 'Increase' has no meaning as a focus 'of the processes'.

key_note: Loosely drafted item: BPR (Hammer and Champy) and Process Innovation (Davenport) date from the early 1990s, not 1999, and standard theory calls BPR radical redesign. 'Amend' is accepted as the examiner's intended word.

topic_name: Themes and findings of the latest Economic Survey
short_explanation: Financialisation describes the growing share of household savings flowing into formal financial instruments such as mutual funds, equities and insurance rather than physical assets. The Economic Survey 2024-25 repeatedly uses this term, noting both the benefits and the risks of rapid financialisation.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Monetisation refers to converting assets or debt into money, not shifting savings into financial instruments.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: De-regulation is about removing rules, not the shift of household savings.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Fiscalisation is not the term used for this shift of savings.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Dollarisation refers to use of a foreign currency, typically the US dollar, in a domestic economy.

common_traps: Monetisation sounds similar but refers to converting assets or debt into money.

short_explanation: The World Population Prospects is the UN's official set of population estimates and projections, prepared by the Population Division of the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs (UN DESA).

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: UNDP publishes the Human Development Report, not the World Population Prospects.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: UNESCO works on education, science and culture and does not publish this report.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: UNICEF publishes the State of the World's Children, not the World Population Prospects.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: WHO publishes health statistics, not the UN population projections.

common_traps: Confusing it with UNFPA's State of World Population report, a different UN population publication.

topic_name: Vroom expectancy theory — valence, instrumentality, expectancy
short_explanation: Vroom's theory says motivation = Expectancy (effort will lead to performance) × Instrumentality (performance will bring the reward) × Valence (how much the reward is valued). A transparent, performance-linked plan with reward choices raises all three.
explanation_text: In the example, transparency and a clear link to performance raise expectancy and instrumentality: employees can see that effort leads to measured performance, and performance to the reward. Letting employees choose bonuses, vouchers or training raises valence, because each person picks the reward they value most. Since the three terms multiply, a zero in any one removes motivation.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Skill variety, task identity and autonomy come from Hackman and Oldham's Job Characteristics Model.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Hygiene and motivational factors are from Herzberg's two-factor theory.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Physiological, safety and esteem needs are levels of Maslow's hierarchy.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Achievement, affiliation and power are McClelland's needs.

common_traps: Each wrong option is a real content or process theory; match the terms to the theorist.

short_explanation: A fund flow statement explains the sources and uses of funds, meaning working capital, between two balance-sheet dates. Its purpose is to analyse changes in the working-capital position.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Cash-flow position is the subject of the cash flow statement.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents are what a cash flow statement (AS 3) reports.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Profitability is measured by the profit and loss account.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Budgets are forward-looking plans; the fund flow statement analyses past changes.

common_traps: 'Funds' here means working capital, not cash; options (a) and (b) describe the cash flow statement.

short_explanation: RBI's Financial Inclusion Index is a composite 0 to 100 measure built on three sub-indices (access, usage and quality) and published each July for the year ending March. For March 2025 it rose to 67.0.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 64.2 was the FI-Index for March 2024, the previous year's reading.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary alternative figure; the March 2025 reading was 67.0.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary alternative figure; the March 2025 reading was 67.0.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary alternative figure; the March 2025 reading was 67.0.

common_traps: Picking 64.2, the March 2024 value, instead of the latest March 2025 reading.

topic_name: Kurt Lewin styles — autocratic, democratic, laissez-faire
short_explanation: Kurt Lewin's 1939 studies identified three leadership styles: autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire. Bureaucratic leadership comes from later classifications drawing on Weber.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Autocratic is one of Lewin's three styles.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Democratic (participative) is one of Lewin's three styles.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Laissez-faire (delegative) is one of Lewin's three styles.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Filler option; a correct answer is present.

topic_name: Cash and cash equivalents — the three-month test
short_explanation: Under AS 3 and Ind AS 7, an investment normally counts as a cash equivalent only if it has a short maturity of three months or less from the date of acquisition.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: One month is stricter than the standard's three-month benchmark.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Two months is not the benchmark; the standard uses three months.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Four months exceeds the three-month benchmark.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Six months exceeds the three-month benchmark.

common_traps: The three months run from the date of acquisition, not from the balance-sheet date.

short_explanation: Job costing suits work done to specific customer orders, each job distinct. Construction is the classic case, costed through contract costing, which is a form of job costing.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Retail trading buys and resells goods; it does not cost production jobs.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Service undertakings as a class use service or operating costing; job costing fits only specific order-based services.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Mass production of identical units uses process or unit costing.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Continuous process manufacturing uses process costing.

common_traps: Treating contract costing as unrelated to job costing: it is job costing applied to large, long-duration jobs.
key_note: Job costing is also used by some service firms (repair shops, printers), but 'Service' as an industry class is linked to operating costing; construction is the intended answer.

short_explanation: Boat speed in still water = 50 - 15 = 35 km/h, so upstream speed = 35 - 15 = 20 km/h. Time = 900/20 + 630/50 = 45 + 12.6 = 57.6 hours.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 72.5 hours; the working gives 57.6 hours (45 + 12.6).

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 68.4 hours; the working gives 57.6 hours (45 + 12.6).

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 70.2 hours; the working gives 57.6 hours (45 + 12.6).

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 48.8 hours; the working gives 57.6 hours (45 + 12.6).

solution_steps: Downstream speed = boat + stream = 50, so boat speed = 50 - 15 = 35 km/h.
Upstream speed = 35 - 15 = 20 km/h.
Upstream time = 900/20 = 45 hours.
Downstream distance = 70% of 900 = 630 km; time = 630/50 = 12.6 hours.
Total = 45 + 12.6 = 57.6 hours.
formula_used: Downstream = b + s; Upstream = b - s; Time = Distance / Speed
common_traps: Taking upstream speed as 50 - 15 = 35 km/h (subtracting the stream only once), which gives about 38.3 hours.
Using the full 900 km for the return journey, which gives 63 hours.

short_explanation: Banks are partnering with solar developers to finance rooftop and captive solar projects for MSMEs, easing their transition to clean energy. Bank of Baroda signed the MoU with Tata Power Renewable Energy for such financing.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Not the company named in the Bank of Baroda MoU.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Not the company named in the Bank of Baroda MoU.

option_rationales.rationale: Not the company named in the Bank of Baroda MoU.

short_explanation: UN population projections show India, already the world's most populous country, growing for about four more decades. It is projected to peak in the early 2060s at around 1.7 billion and then decline gradually, so all three statements are correct.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits Statements 2 and 3; the projected peak is about 1.7 billion, followed by a gradual decline.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits Statement 3; the projections show a gradual decline after the peak.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits Statement 1; the peak is projected around 2062.

option_rationales.label: d

key_note: The UN DESA edition carrying these figures is World Population Prospects 2024; the stem's '2025' label appears to conflate it with UNFPA's 2025 report. The facts themselves support the key.

short_explanation: A market-wide circuit breaker automatically halts trading when a benchmark index (Nifty 50 or Sensex) moves 10%, 15% or 20% in either direction, giving the market a cooling-off period.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: IPOs are a primary-market process unconnected with circuit breakers, which act on secondary-market trading.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: A market-wide circuit breaker halts trading across equity and equity derivative segments, not only F&O.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Circuit breakers apply to all participants, not selectively to foreign investors.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Only the 20% trigger halts trading for the rest of the day; the 10% and 15% triggers cause halts of limited duration, so closure is not automatic in every case.

common_traps: Assuming every circuit-breaker trigger shuts the market for the day; only the 20% level does, and the halt length at 10% and 15% depends on the time of day.

short_explanation: In a defined contribution scheme, contributions are fixed and the pension depends on the market-linked corpus they build. NPS works this way; the other named schemes promise a defined benefit.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The old civil-service pension is a defined benefit, based on last pay and length of service.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: EPS-95 pays a formula-based pension (pensionable salary × service / 70), so it is a defined benefit.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: APY guarantees fixed pension slabs backed by the government, so it is a defined benefit even though it uses NPS architecture.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Traditional annuity plans pay a guaranteed income fixed at purchase; they are not defined contribution schemes.

common_traps: Treating APY as defined contribution because PFRDA administers it through NPS; its pension is guaranteed.

short_explanation: The Expected Credit Loss (ECL) approach, as in IFRS 9, requires lenders to provide for credit losses before they occur, using forward-looking information and probability-weighted scenarios. It replaces the incurred-loss model, under which losses were recognised only once a default or impairment trigger had happened.
explanation_text: Under ECL, exposures are staged: Stage 1 (performing) carries a 12-month expected loss; Stage 2 (significant increase in credit risk) and Stage 3 (credit-impaired) carry lifetime expected losses. Every stage uses forward-looking, probability-weighted estimates, which is the core difference from the incurred-loss model.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Recognising losses only after an asset turns non-performing is the incurred-loss approach that ECL replaces.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Provisioning on incurred losses and historical data alone is backward-looking; ECL adds forward-looking information.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: ECL is an accounting provisioning approach, not solely a tool for meeting Basel III capital ratios.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: ECL covers all exposures, including performing ones through 12-month expected losses, not just stressed or defaulted accounts.

common_traps: Treating ECL as provisioning for defaulted assets only; its defining feature is that losses are provided for before default.
tag_note: Topic should be banking prudential norms / credit-risk provisioning (ECL). The question tests loan-loss accounting under the prudential framework, not budget concepts.

short_explanation: A derivative is a contract whose value depends on the price of an underlying asset, which may be a stock, index, commodity, currency, interest rate or bond.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Government securities are one possible underlying, not the general source of a derivative's value.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Exchange rates underlie only currency derivatives; 'only' makes this too narrow.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Interest rates underlie interest rate derivatives, and are not in general fixed by RBI; this is too narrow and inaccurate.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: The issuer's credit rating matters for credit instruments; a derivative's value comes from its underlying.

tag_note: Topic should be Derivatives basics and definition. The question tests what a derivative is, not the difference between forwards and futures.

topic_name: PPP models and the project sponsoring authority
short_explanation: In India's PPP framework, the Project Sponsoring Authority (the administrative ministry, department or agency owning the project) identifies and conceptualises the project and prepares the proposal and documents for appraisal and approval.
explanation_text: The sponsoring authority stays in charge through the project cycle: it prepares the feasibility study and draft concession agreement, submits the proposal to the appraisal and approval bodies (such as the PPP Appraisal Committee), and then runs the bid process. Approval of the concession agreement rests with the appraisal and approval bodies, and financing is raised by the private concessionaire. The question asks for its primary role, which is originating and preparing the project.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Approval of the proposal and concession agreement is given by the appraisal and approval bodies (such as the PPP Appraisal Committee and the competent authority), not by the sponsor.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: The sponsor does run the bid process after approval, but that follows from its primary role of conceptualising and preparing the project.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Clearances and permissions come from the relevant statutory and regulatory authorities, not from the sponsor as its primary role.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Long-term financing is arranged mainly by the private concessionaire, not the sponsoring authority.

common_traps: Choosing bid evaluation because the sponsor does run the tender; the question asks for its primary role, which is originating and preparing the project.
key_note: Accepted with a reservation: the sponsoring authority also conducts bidding after approval, so option c is not wholly foreign to its role; the 'primary role' wording points to option b.

short_explanation: HRD interventions develop people: training, development for the present role and for future roles, and performance appraisal as a feedback tool. Setting up organisational structures is an organising function, not an HRD intervention.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Training and development is the core HRD intervention.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Developing employees for their current role is an HRD intervention.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Developing employees for future jobs is an HRD intervention.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Performance appraisal is treated as an HRD mechanism, because it identifies development needs.

key_note: Attribution to Drucker is loose; the answer rests on the general distinction between organising and HRD.

short_explanation: FICCI's India Climate Policy and Business Conclave, run through its Centre for Sustainability Leadership, brings together policymakers and industry on climate policy and carbon markets, including the Indian Carbon Market. The 15th edition was held in Hyderabad.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Not the host city of the 15th edition.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Not the host city of the 15th edition.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Not the host city of the 15th edition.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Not the host city of the 15th edition.

short_explanation: An underwriter commits to subscribe to the unsubscribed portion of an issue, up to its underwriting commitment, for an underwriting commission; taking up this shortfall is called devolvement.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Syndicate members collect bids in a book-built issue; they do not commit to take up the unsubscribed portion.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Anchor investors are qualified institutional buyers who subscribe to their own allocation before the issue opens; they do not guarantee the shortfall.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: A depository participant holds and credits dematerialised shares; it plays no underwriting role.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: The registrar processes applications and handles allotment and refunds; it does not take up unsubscribed shares.

short_explanation: Profit is shared in the ratio of capital × time: Chirag 12000 × 12 = 1,44,000 and Naveen 20000 × 9 = 1,80,000, i.e. 4 : 5. Naveen's share = 4320 × 5/9 = Rs.2400.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives Rs.3360; the working gives Rs.2400 (4320 × 5/9).

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives Rs.2880; the working gives Rs.2400 (4320 × 5/9).

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Rs.1920 is Chirag's share (4320 × 4/9), not Naveen's.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives Rs.1440; the working gives Rs.2400 (4320 × 5/9).

solution_steps: Chirag's capital-months = 12000 × 12 = 144000.
Naveen's capital-months = 20000 × 9 = 180000.
Naveen's share = 4320 × 5/9 = Rs.2400.
common_traps: Ignoring the 9 months and splitting 12000 : 20000 = 3 : 5 gives Rs.2700 to Naveen.
Picking the other partner's share (Rs.1920).

short_explanation: Share-based payments are best valued at fair value, i.e. the market-based value of the option or share at grant date. 'Market value' is the option that stands for this recommended basis.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: 'Revalue' is not a valuation method.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Book value ignores what the shares are worth in the market.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Average price is not a recognised method for valuing ESOPs.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: The intrinsic value method (market price minus exercise price) was only a permitted alternative under the older ICAI Guidance Note; the fair or market value approach is the recommended one.

common_traps: Intrinsic value is a real, permitted method, so it looks right; the question asks which method is recommended.
key_note: The ICAI Guidance Note recommends the fair value method; the key's 'Market Value' is read as that basis.

short_explanation: In budget and Economic Survey language, the engines of growth are the components of aggregate demand: private consumption, investment, government spending and exports. Labour is a factor of production on the supply side, not a demand engine.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Private consumption is the largest demand component and is routinely called an engine of growth.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Government spending, especially capital expenditure, is regularly described as a growth engine in budget documents.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Exports are routinely cited as an engine of growth.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Investment (capital formation) is a standard engine of growth.

common_traps: Picking government spending because it is policy-driven; it is still counted as a demand engine.

topic_name: Which costing method suits which industry
short_explanation: Continuous, high-volume production of identical biscuits through successive stages points to process costing, which is the key.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: ABC is an overhead-allocation technique, not a costing method chosen by type of production.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Job costing fits unique customer orders, not identical high-volume output.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Contract costing fits large, site-based construction contracts.

common_traps: Standard textbook lists put biscuits under batch costing; the 'high volume' wording in this stem pushes towards process costing.
key_note: Options (c) Process Costing and (e) Batch Costing are both defensible: the key relies on 'high volume', but ICAI and most Indian costing texts list biscuit manufacturing as the standard example of batch costing.

topic_name: Asset classes E, C, G and A
short_explanation: The NPS asset classes are E (equity), C (corporate debt), G (government securities) and A (alternative investment funds); Scheme G invests mainly in government securities.

option_rationales.label: b

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Scheme E invests mainly in equity.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: There is no Scheme F among NPS asset classes.

common_traps: Reading 'C' as central government; it stands for corporate debt.

short_explanation: Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana was launched in August 2014 as the national mission for financial inclusion, giving every household a basic bank account with a RuPay card and accident insurance cover.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Stand-Up India, for bank loans to SC/ST and women entrepreneurs, was launched in April 2016.

common_traps: The three social-security schemes (PMSBY, PMJJBY, APY) were launched together in 2015 and built on Jan Dhan accounts; they are often mis-dated to 2014.

short_explanation: All three schemes serve the unorganised sector. APY is aimed chiefly at unorganised-sector workers, PM Shram Yogi Maandhan is a pension scheme for unorganised workers, and the Laghu Vyapari Maandhan (NPS-Traders) covers small traders and self-employed persons outside formal pension cover.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: APY alone is incomplete; the paired options show more than one listed scheme is expected, and several qualify.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: PM-SYM does target unorganised workers, but on its own it is incomplete as more than one scheme qualifies.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Laghu Vyapari Maandhan alone is incomplete; other listed schemes also target the unorganised sector.

key_note: Options d (A and C) and e (B and C) are both defensible: PM Shram Yogi Maandhan is explicitly a pension scheme for unorganised workers, so excluding it (key d) has no basis, and APY equally targets the unorganised sector. No option offers all three.

short_explanation: Under media richness theory (Daft and Lengel), ambiguous problems need rich channels with instant feedback, several cues and a personal touch. Face-to-face meetings are the richest channel.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Quarterly reports are lean, one-way and slow, suited to routine data.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Newsletters are lean, one-way broadcasts.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Notice-board circulars are the leanest, impersonal written medium.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Pre-recorded video carries voice and visual cues but allows no real-time feedback, so it is not rich enough.

common_traps: Video seems rich, but without two-way feedback it cannot resolve ambiguity.

short_explanation: Backflush costing, used with JIT, skips tracking work-in-progress. Costs are recorded at the end, when output is completed or sold, and are then 'flushed back' to the units.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Job costing tracks costs for each job as work proceeds, WIP included.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: ABC allocates overhead by activity drivers; it does not remove WIP entries.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Batch costing collects costs for each batch as it is produced.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Contract costing records work-in-progress on each contract.

common_traps: Linking 'no WIP' to JIT and then picking a JIT tool; backflush is the costing method that goes with JIT.

short_explanation: RBI publishes daily payment-system data covering UPI, NEFT, RTGS and other channels. When the rationalised GST rates took effect on 22 September 2025, digital payments that day were reported at around ₹11 trillion, close to ten times the previous day's value.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary alternative figure; the reported value was about ₹11 trillion.

option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary alternative figure; the reported value was about ₹11 trillion.

key_note: The ₹11 trillion figure is accepted from the key; the specific daily RBI value could not be independently corroborated.

topic_name: Leverage ratios — debt-equity and capital gearing
short_explanation: The capital gearing ratio compares fixed-interest or fixed-dividend capital (debentures, long-term loans, preference capital) with equity shareholders' funds.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Debt-to-equity compares debt with total shareholders' funds, preference capital included, not specifically interest-bearing with equity capital.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: The equity ratio compares equity with total assets or capital employed.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: The proprietary ratio compares shareholders' funds with total assets.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: DSCR measures ability to service debt from cash earnings.

formula_used: Capital gearing ratio = (Preference capital + Debentures + Long-term loans) / Equity shareholders' funds
common_traps: Debt-to-equity is a close neighbour; capital gearing specifically puts equity alone in the denominator and all fixed-charge capital in the numerator.

short_explanation: Tri-party repo in government securities is run centrally by the Clearing Corporation of India Ltd (CCIL), which acts as the tri-party agent and central counterparty on its TREPS platform.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: RBI regulates the repo market and conducts its own repo operations, but it does not operate the tri-party repo platform.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: SEBI regulates repo in corporate bonds on exchanges, not the centralised tri-party repo in government securities.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: SIDBI is a development finance institution for MSMEs, with no role in operating tri-party repo.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: NABARD is a development finance institution for agriculture and rural development, with no role in operating tri-party repo.

common_traps: Choosing RBI because it regulates repo and conducts LAF repo; the tri-party platform itself is operated by CCIL.

short_explanation: After 1 year at 6% SI the sum is 2650; two years at 8% CI make it 2650 × 1.1664 = ₹3090.96. The interest of ₹590.96 over 3 years on ₹2500 is a simple rate of 590.96 / 7500 × 100 = 7.88%.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 7.50%; the working gives 7.88% (590.96/7500).

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: 8% is the compound rate for the last two years, not the single equivalent simple rate.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 7.75%; the working gives 7.88% (590.96/7500).

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 7.91%; the working gives 7.88% (590.96/7500).

solution_steps: Amount after year 1 = 2500 × 1.06 = ₹2650.
Amount after 2 more years at 8% CI = 2650 × 1.08² = 2650 × 1.1664 = ₹3090.96.
common_traps: Averaging the rates (6 + 8 + 8)/3 = 7.33%, which ignores compounding.
Applying the 8% compound interest to the original ₹2500 instead of the ₹2650 carried forward (gives about 7.55%).

short_explanation: NPS is a defined contribution scheme: what is paid in is fixed, and the eventual pension depends on the market-linked corpus it builds. The other named schemes promise a benefit fixed by formula.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The old civil-service pension is a defined benefit, linked to last pay and years of service.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: EPS-95 pays a formula-based pension (pensionable salary × service / 70), so it is a defined benefit.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: A traditional corporate DB pension is by definition a defined benefit.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Fails because options a, b and d are all defined benefit schemes.

common_traps: Being drawn to 'All of the above' without checking that every other listed scheme is defined benefit.

short_explanation: AS 2 values inventory at the lower of cost and net realisable value. NRV = 6,042 − 4% brokerage (241.68) − 1,000 to complete = ₹4,800.32. That is below the cost of ₹5,000, so closing inventory is ₹4,800.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: ₹4,000 wrongly deducts the ₹1,000 completion cost from the cost of ₹5,000 instead of from the selling price.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: ₹4,500 does not follow from any step of the calculation.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: ₹5,000 is the cost; it ignores the lower-of-cost-or-NRV test, which NRV of ₹4,800 fails.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: ₹5,500 does not follow from any step of the calculation.

solution_steps: Net realisable value = 6,042 − 241.68 − 1,000 (cost to complete) = ₹4,800.32.
Cost of partly finished goods = ₹5,000.
Inventory = lower of cost and NRV = lower of 5,000 and 4,800 = ₹4,800.
formula_used: Inventory = Lower of Cost and NRV; NRV = Estimated selling price − Costs to complete − Costs to sell
common_traps: Adding the ₹1,000 completion cost to the ₹5,000 cost; completion cost reduces NRV, it does not raise cost.
Forgetting the brokerage, which gives NRV of ₹5,042 and wrongly values the goods at cost.

short_explanation: Just-in-Time means materials are bought and goods produced only when demand requires them, which keeps inventory close to zero.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: EOQ sets an optimal order size to minimise ordering and carrying costs; it does not wait for demand.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: MRP schedules material needs from a production plan and forecasts, typically buying ahead of use.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Kaizen is continuous incremental improvement, not a purchasing rule.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Six Sigma reduces process variation and defects.

common_traps: MRP also plans material needs but is push-based and forecast-driven; JIT is pull-based.

topic_name: Koontz and O'Donnell on the manager's function
short_explanation: Koontz and O'Donnell define management as getting things done through and with people in formally organised groups, i.e. achieving common objectives through others' effort.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Long-term strategic planning is one function a manager performs, not the defining one.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Controlling behaviour is a single function and too narrow.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Designing structure is part of organising, only one function.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Preparing financial reports is a specialist task, not the manager's essential role.

common_traps: Mary Parker Follett's 'art of getting things done through people' is often mixed up with this; the essence is the same.

topic_name: Number series — arithmetic and difference patterns
short_explanation: The differences double each time: 11, 22, 44, 88, so the next difference is 176 and the missing term is 388 + 176 = 564.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 456; the working gives 564 (388 + 176).

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 465; the working gives 564 (388 + 176).

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 524; the working gives 564 (388 + 176).

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 488; the working gives 564 (388 + 176).

solution_steps: Each difference is twice the previous, so next = 176.
Missing term = 388 + 176 = 564.

short_explanation: The Cheque Truncation System clears cheques by sending their electronic images instead of the paper, which used to be settled in fixed batches. RBI's revision, effective 4 October 2025, moved CTS to continuous clearing, with cheques scanned and presented through the day and settled on realisation, cutting clearing time to a matter of hours.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Automation of clearing happened well before CTS; the 2025 change is about the timing of clearing and settlement.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Grid-based CTS already consolidated clearing nationally; the 2025 change is not a regional-to-national shift.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Moving from physical cheques to image-based clearing was the original CTS reform, not the 2025 change.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: The change brings continuous clearing with settlement on realisation, not a switch limited to intraday settlement.

common_traps: Choosing paper-to-image clearing, which describes the original CTS rollout and not the October 2025 move from batch to continuous clearing.

topic_name: Poverty alleviation and employment generation in India
short_explanation: Jal Jeevan Mission, launched in 2019, aims to provide every rural household with a functional tap water connection. Its original 2024 deadline was extended, and the Union Budget 2025-26 extended the mission to 2028.

short_explanation: In the interbank money market, call money is for overnight (one day), notice money for 2 to 14 days, and term money for 15 days up to one year.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Overnight funds are call money, not notice money.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: 15 to 30 days falls within term money (15 days up to one year).

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Above one year is outside the money market altogether.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: 3 to 6 months falls within term money, not notice money.

topic_name: Poverty alleviation and employment generation in India
short_explanation: The World Bank's Poverty and Equity Brief for India estimated extreme poverty (at $2.15 a day) at 2.3% in 2022-23, down from about 16% in 2011-12. Poverty fell in both rural and urban areas, so Statement 2 is wrong, while employment growth has outpaced growth of the working-age population since 2021-22.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits Statement 3, which the brief also reported.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 2 is wrong: poverty fell in urban areas as well as rural areas.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits Statement 1; the 2.3% extreme-poverty estimate is correct.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Includes Statement 2, which is wrong because urban poverty also declined.

common_traps: Assuming urban poverty rose because of migration; the brief shows declines in both rural and urban poverty.

topic_name: Introduction to cost and management accounting
short_explanation: Cost analysis means examining a cost, breaking it down into components such as material, labour and overhead, and evaluating what drives each one.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Estimating future prices is forecasting or pricing, not cost analysis.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Comparing actual and budgeted results is variance analysis or budgetary control.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Calculating taxes is tax computation.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Studying consumer demand is demand analysis in economics or marketing.

common_traps: Option (b) is a close neighbour: variance analysis is one use of cost data, but cost analysis itself is about the make-up of cost.

short_explanation: An interest rate swap exchanges fixed-rate for floating-rate interest payments on a notional principal, letting an institution change its exposure to rate movements. It is the standard hedge for interest rate risk among the options.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Nifty futures hedge equity market risk, not interest rate risk.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Gap analysis measures interest rate risk by comparing rate-sensitive assets and liabilities; it identifies the exposure but is not a hedging instrument.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Equity options hedge share price risk, not interest rate risk.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Commodity forwards hedge commodity price risk, not interest rate risk.

common_traps: Choosing 'Gap' because gap analysis appears in ALM discussions of interest rate risk; it is a measurement tool, not a hedge.
key_note: Reservation: gap management (repricing assets and liabilities) is also an ALM way to manage interest rate risk, but the bare word 'Gap' names the measure of exposure, and interest rate swaps are the clear hedging instrument.

topic_name: AS 11 — foreign exchange, FCMITDA, non-integrated operations
short_explanation: Under para 46A of AS 11, exchange differences on long-term foreign-currency monetary items not related to depreciable assets are held in the FCMITDA. The balance is shown in the balance sheet as a separate line under 'Reserves and Surplus', which is the keyed answer.
explanation_text: Para 46A was an optional relief: instead of taking long-term foreign-currency exchange differences straight to profit and loss, an entity could add those on depreciable assets to the asset's cost, and hold the rest in the FCMITDA. The FCMITDA is amortised to profit and loss over the remaining life of the asset or liability. Its unamortised balance is shown on the balance sheet under Reserves and Surplus, a negative figure when it is a debit.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: FCMITDA is an equity-side adjustment account, not a current liability.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Exchange differences never go to share capital.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: FCMITDA is not a deferred tax balance; deferred tax is dealt with under AS 22.

common_traps: Mixing up where the FCMITDA balance sits (Reserves and Surplus) with where it is amortised to (Profit and Loss).
key_note: Options (a) Profit and Loss Account and (e) Reserves and Surplus are both defensible: para 46A amortises the FCMITDA balance to the Statement of Profit and Loss over the item's remaining life, while the unamortised balance is presented under Reserves and Surplus. 'Transferred to' fits the amortisation better, 'shown under' the key.

topic_name: Number series — multiplicative and mixed patterns
short_explanation: Each term is (previous × n) + n with n = 1, 2, 3, ...: 23×1+1 = 24, 24×2+2 = 50, 50×3+3 = 153, so the missing term is 153×4+4 = 616, and 616×5+5 = 3085 confirms it.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 600; the working gives 616 (153 × 4 + 4).

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 500; the working gives 616 (153 × 4 + 4).

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 400; the working gives 616 (153 × 4 + 4).

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 515; the working gives 616 (153 × 4 + 4).

common_traps: Stopping at 153 × 4 = 612 and forgetting to add the 4 (612 is not offered, but it signals the missed step).

short_explanation: Mittelstand is the German term for the country's small and medium-sized, often family-owned, enterprises that form the backbone of its manufacturing and exports. In the Indian context it corresponds to the SME/medium-enterprise segment, the 'missing middle' policymakers want to grow.

option_rationales.label: b

option_rationales.label: d

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: The Mittelstand consists of formal, established firms, not the informal sector.

short_explanation: Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) is the integrated information system that management uses to monitor and run day-to-day operations such as finance, HR, inventory and production.

short_explanation: Life insurance business in India was nationalised in 1956: an ordinance took over management in January, and LIC was established on 1 September 1956 under the LIC Act, 1956.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: 1952 is not linked to life insurance nationalisation.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 1969 is when 14 major commercial banks were nationalised.

short_explanation: Under AS 22, deferred tax arises only from timing differences, which reverse in later periods. Penalties and fines are disallowed permanently for tax, so they are permanent differences and create no deferred tax.

option_rationales.label: d

common_traps: Permanent differences (fines, penalties, exempt income) never reverse, so they create no deferred tax.

short_explanation: The principle of indemnity puts the insured back in the financial position held just before the loss, no better and no worse, so insurance cannot be a source of profit.

topic_name: Quadratic equations — root comparison (x vs y)
short_explanation: x² - 21x + 68 = 0 gives x = 4 or 17; 2y² + 11y - 63 = 0 gives y = 3.5 or -9. Every x-root exceeds every y-root, so x > y.

option_rationales.rationale: Too weak: x and y are never equal, so the strict relation x > y is the answer.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: The largest y (3.5) is below the smallest x (4).

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: A definite relation holds, so this does not apply.

solution_steps: Smallest x (4) > largest y (3.5).
Hence x > y.
common_traps: Forgetting to divide by 2a for 2y², giving y = 7 and concluding the relation cannot be established.

topic_name: Digital Public Infrastructure and India Stack
short_explanation: Zero-trust architecture drops the idea of a trusted internal network. Every user, device and request is authenticated and authorised each time, whether it comes from inside or outside, summed up as 'never trust, always verify'.

short_explanation: O and P have one person (R) between them. In the solved order R-S, U-Q, M-T and P-U also have exactly one person between them, so four options fit.
explanation_text: The order that satisfies the premises (with the U/Q clue read as 'at least three before Q and at least three after U') is O (Mar 9), R (Mar 26), P (Apr 9), S (Apr 26), U (Jun 9), N (Jun 26), Q (Jul 9), T (Jul 26), V (Sep 9), M (Sep 26). The natural reading of that clue, U before Q with three or more between, has no solution.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: V (Sep 9) and N (Jun 26) have two people, Q and T, between them.

solution_steps: Slots: 1 Mar 9, 2 Mar 26, 3 Apr 9, 4 Apr 26, 5 Jun 9, 6 Jun 26, 7 Jul 9, 8 Jul 26, 9 Sep 9, 10 Sep 26.
P is in April, R in an earlier month (March) and M in a later month. O is four months before T on an odd date: O Mar 9 (T in July), so R is Mar 26 and V (different date from R) is on a 9th.

If U must come before Q with at least three people between them, no arrangement exists: Q (31-day month) can only be July, U would have to be April with N, but April already holds P. Reading the clue as 'at least three before Q and at least three after U' gives a solution.
Q takes Jul 9 and T Jul 26. S is four slots from T: S = Apr 26, so P = Apr 9 and U (same date as P, same month as N, after S's month) = Jun 9, N = Jun 26.
V is on a 9th with at least three people between V and U: V = Sep 9, M = Sep 26.
Unique order: O, R, P, S, U, N, Q, T, V, M.
key_note: Under the natural reading of the U/Q clue the premises have no solution; under the only workable reading the order is O, R, P, S, U, N, Q, T, V, M. O-P has one person between; so do R-S (P), U-Q (N), T-M (V) and P-U (S). Competing options: a, b, c and e.

short_explanation: May Earbuds = 3/5 of 1500 = 900, which is 44% more than April, so April = 900/1.44 = 625. June Earbuds = 11/15 of 1500 = 1100. Total April to June = 625 + 900 + 1100 = 2625.
explanation_text: The table gives the average of Power bank and Earbuds sales for each month, so the month's combined sale is twice that figure, which is then split in the given ratio: May 600/900, June 400/1100, July 650/350, August 750/450, September 300/500, October 500/600 (Power bank/Earbuds).

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 2500; the working gives 2625 (625 + 900 + 1100).

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 2275; the working gives 2625 (625 + 900 + 1100).

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 2100; the working gives 2625 (625 + 900 + 1100).

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 2945; the working gives 2625 (625 + 900 + 1100).

solution_steps: Combined sale = 2 × average: May = 1500, June = 1500.
May Earbuds = 1500 × 3/5 = 900; June Earbuds = 1500 × 11/15 = 1100.
April Earbuds = 900 / 1.44 = 625.
common_traps: Taking April as 56% of May (900 × 0.56 = 504), i.e. subtracting 44% from May instead of dividing by 1.44; that gives 2504.
Using the table average as the combined sale, which halves every figure.

short_explanation: The statement reports only that parents found the fee too high and the school responded. It need not assume that parents will now pay willingly (I) or that they previously refused to pay (II): finding a fee high is not the same as being unwilling to pay it.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The decision responds to feedback; it does not rest on predicting that parents will now become willing payers.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: 'Find the fee too high' does not mean parents were unwilling to pay; they may have paid while complaining.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Either-or needs two complementary assumptions, one of which must hold; neither is needed here.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Neither assumption is required for the statement to make sense.

common_traps: Equating 'finds the fee too high' with 'refused to pay' (II).
key_note: Assumption I is sometimes treated as implicit (an action assumes it will achieve its purpose), but the statement frames the cut as a response to feedback, not a bid to raise payment, which supports the key.

short_explanation: RBI's Payments Vision 2025 relies on digital technologies, including artificial intelligence and data analytics, to make e-payments available to everyone, everywhere, every time.

option_rationales.label: b

option_rationales.label: d

option_rationales.label: e

short_explanation: An NBFC is a company registered under the Companies Act that carries on lending, investment in securities, leasing or hire-purchase (Statement 1). RBI's principal-business test classifies it as an NBFC when financial assets exceed 50% of total assets and financial income exceeds 50% of gross income (Statement 2). Statement 3 is wrong, because companies whose principal business is agriculture, industry or immovable property are expressly excluded from NBFC registration.
explanation_text: Section 45-I(f) of the RBI Act, 1934 defines a non-banking financial company. Registration under Section 45-IA applies where financial business is the principal business, judged by the 50-50 test. Institutions whose principal business is agricultural activity, industrial activity, trading in goods (other than securities), services, or the purchase, sale or construction of immovable property are excluded.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes Statement 3, which reverses the exclusion: such businesses do not need NBFC registration.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits Statement 2, the correct 50-50 principal-business test.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Omits Statement 1, the correct basic definition of an NBFC.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Includes Statement 3, which is wrong because those businesses are excluded from NBFC registration.

common_traps: Reading Statement 3 as a list of NBFC activities; it is the RBI Act's list of exclusions.
tag_note: Topic should be banking and NBFC regulation. The question tests the statutory definition and principal-business test for NBFCs, not a current event.

short_explanation: Power bank sale in August = 5/8 of 1200 = 750 and in September = 3/8 of 800 = 300. The fall is 450 on a base of 750, i.e. a 60% decrease.
explanation_text: The table gives the average of Power bank and Earbuds sales for each month, so the month's combined sale is twice that figure, which is then split in the given ratio: May 600/900, June 400/1100, July 650/350, August 750/450, September 300/500, October 500/600 (Power bank/Earbuds).

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 40% is September's sale as a percentage of August's (300/750), not the percentage change.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 30%; the working gives a 60% decrease (750 to 300).

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 75%; the working gives a 60% decrease (750 to 300).

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 55%; the working gives a 60% decrease (750 to 300).

solution_steps: August combined = 2 × 600 = 1200; Power bank = 1200 × 5/8 = 750.
September combined = 2 × 400 = 800; Power bank = 800 × 3/8 = 300.
Change = 750 - 300 = 450 (decrease).
Percentage decrease = 450/750 × 100 = 60%.
common_traps: Reporting 300/750 = 40% (the ratio) instead of the 60% fall.
Using September (300) as the base, which gives 150%.

topic_name: Statement and argument — strong or weak
short_explanation: Argument I gives a direct, relevant benefit of the policy. Argument II assumes one activity would overload students who are struggling academically; that concern is limited to a subset and not a decisive reason against the policy.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: II covers only students already struggling and assumes a single activity adds decisive pressure, so it is weak.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: II is weak, so both cannot be strong.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Either-or applies only to two equally valid, opposed arguments; here only I is strong.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: I is a strong, directly relevant reason.

common_traps: Treating any stated disadvantage as a strong argument without checking how far it reaches.
key_note: II raises a real concern and some would call it strong too (both strong); the key treats it as limited in scope.

short_explanation: 'Pink tax' is not a legal levy. It describes the price premium often charged on products and services marketed to women, such as razors, personal-care items and dry cleaning, compared with near-identical versions marketed to men.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: There is no official tax on pink-coloured goods; the term is metaphorical.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: It is not an excise or customs duty; it arises from pricing, not government levies.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: It is not a GST levy; sanitary napkins have in fact been GST-exempt in India since 2018.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: It refers to higher prices for comparable products, not higher manufacturing labour costs.

common_traps: Taking 'tax' literally; the pink tax is a pricing disparity, not a government levy.
